situation:
You finished school last spring and you are three months into your first salaried job. Your benefits enrollment window closes on Friday. This afternoon you are meeting a benefits counselor (judge) from HALVERSON BENEFIT ADVISORS, the firm brought in to walk new hires through the coverage they may elect.

The family car you share with your mother needs a transmission repair that costs $2,400, and the car itself is worth about $1,700. You have $1,500 in cash and nothing more set aside. Your mother co-signed your student loan and drives that car to her own job every morning.

During enrollment you may elect disability coverage for $19 a month and a small term life policy for $11 a month, or decline both. If an injury kept you from working, or if you died, the student loan payments would fall to your mother, who has no other way to cover them.

Paying the repair with your $1,500 in cash and putting the remaining $900 on a credit card would let you keep both coverages, but the card balance would carry for months at a high rate. The repair shop also offers a loan against the car title, and taking it would close the $900 shortfall the same day, at a rate high enough that one missed payment would be reported and damage your credit record.

The counselor (judge) wants your recommendation on the repair and on the coverage. The counselor (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, then thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are a benefits counselor from HALVERSON BENEFIT ADVISORS. Business background is the same as the situation above.

A new hire three months into a first salaried job is choosing coverage during an enrollment window that closes Friday, while a shared family car needs a repair that costs more than the car is worth. You want to hear which coverages this new hire should elect, what an injury or a death would mean for the mother who co-signed the student loan, and a clear recommendation on paying for the repair.

After the participant has presented, you are to ask the following questions of each participant:
judgeQuestions: If you had gone the other way, what would that have cost you?
What would have to change for you to make the opposite choice?
